notes.title: Devlog 80
notes.notes: [p]Still adjusting to married life and doing a lot of outside stuff, so I haven't had as much time as I would have liked. I will apply myself more diligently in the coming weeks and get out an update with some new quests soon, but I want to share what I have been working on now.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/97fd700a61c5055b3c3bff78a250b6d7218d6ecd.png"][/img][i]Food! Just sitting there![/i][/p][p]In retrospect it seems both simple and complicated, oddly enough. I had the idea for the global reset system ages ago when working on NPC mobs in towns, since it would be strange for them to find them sleeping in the middle of the day and they all suddenly wake up and go to work. The reset system moves them to appropriate areas and doing appropriate actions throughout the day, and is distributed over time so that it doesn't lag the game out by processing everything at once.[/p][p][/p][p]In addition, once per day, new items spawn in the various biome features (and old items are deleted). I also created a system that resets all lair encounters. This not only allows you to traverse lairs multiple times and experience new encounters, traps, loot, and monsters, but also amps up the difficulty as you progress since it generates multiple times in the playthrough. This is a new feature, and while planned for a while, hadn't really been added. Previously, everything was ad hoc, so in theory lairs could all be generated for a level 1 player and disposed of at leisure.[/p][p][/p][p]And finally I'm beginning work on the monster hunt quest. This means something I really didn't like doing: delving back into my elegant but persnickety conversation interface. To say that it was held together by duck tape and paper clips is an understatement; I will have to do a lot of tuning to get it back to an operational state what with the new quest system. I might even have to make a small utility to be able to create conversations faster. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to [url="https://roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com"]roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com[/url], or just leave them in the comments below.[/p][p][/p]

notes.title: Devlog 79 / Update 0.2.79a
notes.notes:
[p]Before we begin, a life announcement! I got married two weeks ago! Yes, that has contributed to a little bit of neglect on my part for Rogues of Europa, but I don't regret it.[/p][p][/p][p]I started working a bit on some of the new oddjob quests, particularly "seek and destroy" quests. These are, as I have mentioned, the second step up the ladder of quests, adding a bit more functionality in terms of quest givers, different subordinate objectives (in this case, killing a particular monster). I have developed many new item panels to this end, and started with some implementation.[/p][p][/p][p]As I was implementing the quests I went on several tangents, but they were useful tangents indeed. For one, I noticed that the features (generally where quests will happen) were far too far apart. My initial solution was to generate more features, but I decided to just add a few more types of feature as well. I added a lava lake feature (called a cauldron because that just sounds way cooler and I needed a one-word name for the feature), as well as a petrified forest (called a petra for similar reasons). I also added a dome feature, which is just a blank space, but still interesting in its own right. None of these were too ground-breaking, and in fact were very quick to implement, but increase the variability of the game significantly.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/7e5cdd79f9afd9c3680a66827e4d1ce8130b6372.png"][/img][i]The cauldron. I may add some animated patches in the future.[/i][/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/3760a3eb6c466a4cc16d2abc59053fd67a2752c8.png"][/img][i]The petra. [/i][/p][p]
These new features will fit into my long term plan of something I call the global reset system. Initially this system was to be designed to make sure NPCs are in the right place at the right time, but this system will also put certain low-level drops in different areas. For example, forests will be good places to find food, and a cauldron might be a great place to find throwing rocks. This will allow you to stock up while exploring, which will be great in a pinch if you have a small pack of rat-men in pursuit.[/p][p][/p][p]Which brings me to the next feature added: more mobs. Doing a quest shouldn't be a slog, but it shouldn't be a breeze either. A good amount of combat interruptions will keep you on your toes. The group behavior is still a bit primitive, but monsters can still easily surround you and start punching down your health quickly.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/255f5e1d634861bb2256fb505b3485608af8ea5b.png"][/img][i]They do move in herds![/i][/p][p]Getting the movement right was a challenge but I at least stopped it from hanging, crashing, or lagging, which is positive. Tell me if you notice any wild behavior, and I'll try to lock that down.[/p][p][/p][p]Mobs also have a few drops now: coins, ammo, and tonics. My initial idea for ammo is to have a "fair" ammo drop, where monsters only drop ammunition you can use. In theory, you can "farm" ammunition of a certain type by dropping your weapons in town and killing monsters, but I have my doubts about how practical this would be (as opposed to just doing things). I will have to play around with balance a bit. Perhaps the derringer, as pathetic as it is, is too overpowered with its two shots, and I'll replace it with the pipe pistol. 20 might be too much ammo now, and I also might need to raise ammo prices. But we will see about that.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/45761eb506d4aaff8e91653b34039a9ec940270e.png"][/img][i]Every penny counts.[/i][/p][p][/p][p]Finally, I added a fullscreen feature that was requested in the forums. I want the ratios to stay very much the same to maintain the look of a 4:3 monitor/command terminal, so I letterboxed the fullscreen based on the size of the screen it's currently in and the UI scale. Tell me if you have any issues with it, I'm not a big company or anything so I can't test it on a UHD monitor, a tiny laptop, the weird extremely wide curved ones, or the like.[/p][p][/p][p]In the coming week, I will probably make a few minor fixes as they crop up and begin more earnest work on the oddjob quests and the global reset system. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to [url="https://roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com"]roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com[/url], or just leave them in the comments below.[/p][p][/p][p][/p][h2]Changes[/h2][list][*][p]New cave feature: Cauldron - a lake of lava[/p][/*][*][p]New cave feature: Petra - a forest of stone and stalactites[/p][/*][*][p]New cave feature: Dome - a broad, empty cavern[/p][/*][*][p]Features spawn far more frequently[/p][/*][*][p]Added XP rewards for exploration[/p][/*][*][p]Mobs spawn far more frequently[/p][/*][*][p]Added mob drops - coins, appropriate ammunition, and tonics[/p][/*][*][p]Added focused-fullscreen mode[/p][/*][*][p]Mobs now spawn in small packs and maintain group cohesion[/p][/*][*][p]Added alert when quest added[/p][/*][*][p]Balance improvements[/p][/*][*][p]Weapon condition reduction reduced significantly[/p][/*][*][p]Healing improved significantly[/p][/*][/list][h2]Bugfixes[/h2][list][*][p]General bugfixes regarding mob behavior[/p][/*][*][p]Fixed some crash conditions[/p][/*][*][p]Fixed some issues with crashes in lairs[/p][/*][/list][h2]Known Issues[/h2][list][*][p]Mouse travels outside hot area in fullscreen mode[/p][/*][*][p]Quest items are too visible when generating in lairs[/p][/*][/list]

notes.title: Devlog 78 / Update 0.2.78a
notes.notes: [h3]Changes[/h3][list][*][p]Added omnivator stations to towns[/p][/*][*][p]Added "Fix Omnivator" quests[/p][/*][*][p]Added quest items[/p][/*][*][p]Revamped quest log[/p][/*][/list][h3]Bugfixes[/h3][list][*][p]Fixed a rare glitch where towns wouldn't generate properly[/p][/*][*][p]Fixed a bug where signposts were automatically targeted[/p][/*][/list][h3]Known Issues[/h3][list][*][p]Omnivators will not work till an update later this week[/p][/*][/list][h3]Devlog[/h3][p]Finally got the omnivator quests done, and I did them the right way. Not only will they be effective quests in their own right, but they are going to form the simple structural basis for the remainder of quests.[/p][p][/p][p]I don't want to dive too much into the backend because it isn't too interesting to the average person, but it should be able to briefly be described through the frontend.[/p][carousel autoadvance="true"][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/cb5e83deae7db55812fc4889bfc9bf793443e185.png"][/img][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/40e55f7b85c012aeae997f6a06f432124d5c353a.png"][/img][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/68ed6107ae431d4d8c5d089ea2ea33f5c55a9da5.png"][/img][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/4aa7120c30f7bd00558d76a197d101e2103047f4.png"][/img][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/4e069ac07fa1fda6e903356ef885885f8f8d0ec8.png"][/img][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/e0ea8fb01c803ebf6aa53dd4a3a6055876e2febd.png"][/img][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/02a2ede923b02b7cc69ff81fa202f862ef5083a4.png"][/img][/carousel][p][i]The quest structure, as explained through frontend images[/i][/p][p][/p][p]Essentially, all quests are divided into objectives of certain types. This makes them highly modular (and maybe in the future, moddable). The left side of the book documents your current objective progress, as well as clues or tips towards finishing the objective.[/p][p][/p][p]The flow of the quest is to find certain items in the surrounding area and bring them back to the omnivator station. After you bring them back, you can attempt to repair the omnivator. Success will unlock the omnivator station in the network and finish the quest, failure will require you to find more items and repeat the process.[/p][p][/p][p]The basic idea of this quest is to encourage exploration of the local area and unlock fast travel using the omnivator network, but it also is a great proof-of-concept for the new quest structure. The state-objective structure will be a much better long-term solution than the previous progress-based structure because it is more flexible, flexible enough to change and add objectives on the fly to create more complex, branching quests. Sure, the single branch here doesn't look like much but I think it shows a lot of promise.[/p][p][/p][p]So for next week: expect actual omnivator fast travel functionality, and starting some new quests, which will take the form of odd jobs done for townspeople. This will be the second important step on the ladder of creating quests. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to [url="https://roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com"]roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com[/url], or just leave them in the comments below.[/p][p][/p]

notes.title: Devlog 77
notes.notes: [p]I continue to plug away at the new quest system, and I think I've got the bones of it in a good place right now.[/p][p][/p][p]Rather than innovate too much I just copied some of my existing systems and what a few other games do and have a state-driven quest system. Basically this functions like a finite-state machine: there are a variety of possible states and rules for going from state to state. But that's just the boring backend.[/p][p][/p][p]Much like with the NPCs, I focused on making a baseline that all other things of that type could be based off of. In the case of NPCs, this was the pig. In the case of quests, it is the omnivator quest, a relatively simple exploration/fetch quest that will unlock fast travel between towns.[/p][p][/p][p]In order to access it, you need to find the new omnivator station building. An omnivator is like an elevator, except it goes sideways as well as up and down.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/53940a4bdc592277209a4c61b933239e4f945267.png"][/img][i]The machinery is a ticket dispenser.[/i][/p][p][/p][p]Once you have finished the quest and unlocked the omnivator, you will be able to use the ticket machine to travel between towns. However, if it is still broken, you'll see the following, and automatically unlock a quest:[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/10185b6439671531a4a62317e1b936f5b01fe4e1.png"][/img][i]It reminds me of Japan, in a way.[/i][/p][p][/p][p]The quest display screen has been updated to a journal, rather than the old abstract system. Slowly skeuomorphism is taking over the game's systems, and I've developed a bit of a liking to it. There's something to be said about computer games being simulacra of tabletop games, which themselves are simulations of real-life or fantasy environs. Skeuomorphism brings the stage back to simulation from simulacrum. My goal with this project was always to put pre-modern art in a post-modern medium, so this scratches that itch.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/7f864ac813f29a1e2a717674e09399788368d50a.png"][/img][i]While it's not yet implemented, soon quests will be organized into supertypes and will be far easier to navigate than the old abstract system.[/i][/p][p][/p][p]Speaking of goals, it is my goal to finish the game by the end of the year. You heard it here first.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/13895160feed683e9098e0b97030998dce1da16b.png"][/img][i]You'll technically have a few more clicks to reach the quest detail screen but I think it's worth it to eliminate scrolling.[/i][/p][p][/p][p]The quest detail needs a bit of fleshing out but I think it looks pretty nice. The checkboxes will get filled in, obviously. I'll probably add a map view or a few pictures to the other side of the journal.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/4fe595419d45ce3d6596eb05e1f87b5867172df6.png"][/img][i]The fact that "Woodale" is next to three different woods is not a part of any system; it was a total coincidence and I thought it was funny.[/i][/p][p][/p][p]There's a lot of behind-the-scenes here that makes this the baseline of all quests, but rest assured it should make quests more modular and therefore easier to produce (and faster to produce). For example, you can see how there could be more choices for the quest type as well as different things listed on the detail page, progress checkboxes rather than item checkboxes, etc. Of course, other quests will be more complex, with things like time sensitivity, companions, interactions with people, different states, branching paths depending on choices and so on.[/p][p][/p][p]I'll have an update out by next week, so keep an eye out for that. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to [url="https://roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com"]roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com[/url], or just leave them in the comments below.[/p]

notes.title: Devlog 76
notes.notes: [p]It's been a while... I haven't been working as diligently as I should have been.[/p][p][/p][p]Over the past few weeks I've mainly been working on creating the dynamic NPC system. The broad stroke of the idea is to have towns feel alive with activity; people working on farms, children running around playing, etc., and avoid the common problem of NPCs having "no life" and just working all the time.[/p][p][/p][p]There are a couple drawbacks to this. The main one is resource consumption. I can't have 30 NPCs all using A* at the same instant, otherwise when delay actions happen (such as waiting, reloading, eating) things slow to a crawl. The second one is that things have to make sense. People can't just be walking randomly all over the place.[/p][p][/p][p]I was bouncing between these two extremes for a few weeks. But I managed to settle on a relatively resource non-intensive way to make things make sense. My solution is to use A* for short bursts and interspersed, while using a heuristic for other pathing.[/p][p][/p][p]I was forced to add the heuristic, pathing, and scheduling all at once, and this led to a whole bunch of bugs for which the source couldn't easily be found. I think I got them all nailed down, though. The end state is that people are able to travel from building to building, regardless of the distance between buildings, and will use the footpaths. I'll probably tweak a few things, but I'm pretty happy with how things are with this functionality.[/p][carousel autoadvance="true"][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/2f800b01fde3cea715e8f923118aa589c38f3703.png"][/img][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/07d42f001ddae21ee429e485d313e0bbd6a827e1.png"][/img][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/6e4a41ba3959854ba28b3b58221a9622182d83e5.png"][/img][/carousel][p][i]The inkeeper and shopkeeper walking to work[/i][/p][p][/p][p]This functionality will allow for all townspeople to do what they need to all day: head to work, head to the inn for a drink and a game of whist, go shopping, visit neighbors, and go home at the end of the day.[/p][p][/p][p]I should be able to push out an update soon with this. Things may be a bit unbalanced for some time as I adjust the NPC behavior (particularly the times when shops are open and closed) but I can always modify things later. And of course quests should be coming soon. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to [url="https://roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com"]roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com[/url], or just leave them in the comments below.[/p][p][/p]

notes.title: Update 0.2.75a / Devlog 75
notes.notes:
[h3]Changes[/h3]
[list]
[*] Readded stores

[*] Changed town generation. Towns are guaranteed to have at least a food store, and additional stores if they have sufficient population
[*] Implemented dice whist as a playable minigame at inns

[/list]


[h3]Bugfixes[/h3]
[list]
[*] Fixed a crash when dropping the last item on the list of inventory items
[*] Ranged weapons no longer lose their bullets when dropped
[/list]

These last couple weeks had some personal difficulties for me, but I persevered a bit and I think I made some good progress. I'm still working on a bit of the infrastructure to allow quests to be added back in, which is primarily based in improving towns.

You as the player will now have a more sensible experience in towns. Each town will now have one food store (unlike before where half of the stores were food stores). Each town will also have an inn, which allows the player to sleep. Additional stores will be based on population of the town. There will still be differences between towns but they should be slighter.

As a fun mini project for me, I created a new minigame to play at inns, called dice cricket. The rules are something like a cross between darts cricket and Yahtzee. There are nine scoring categories, the numbers 1-6, and the three dice suits from whist: keys, coins, and mushrooms. You earn a hit in a category by getting at least three of a kind for numbers, or getting five matching suits, and you have three rolls to accomplish this. You can get additional hits by getting more of a kind or additional matching suits. In order to score, you must first get three hits to open the category. Once you have opened a category, you score points by hitting it again: 10 plus the number for the number categories, 16 for keys, 14 for coins, and 12 for mushrooms. Your opponent can stop you from scoring in a category by scoring at least three hits to close it. The game is over once the player in the lead has opened (or closed) all categories.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/7f18421b97b40040d8a25f53eb48fc90b04007b9.png[/img]
[i]Note the cricket notation in the minigame. It is possible (though rare) to score in two categories at once.[/i]

Finally, I added pigs to the game. This may not sound significant, but it will form the backbone of future mob behavior. Right now the pigs wait around, and walk inside their pens. All future mob behavior will be adding complexity to this, whether it is more states for the mobs to be in (searching, working, traveling) or more complex behavior to accomplish in the states (actually pathing, fighting, etc).
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/48fe1c41a30dd9b1580102c313a445ad9d885d70.png[/img]
[i]It's not much, but it's honest work.[/i]

Next few weeks, it will be mostly if not entirely creating mob behavior. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com, or just leave them in the comments below.

notes.title: Devlog 73
notes.notes:
I was relatively busy this week after work, so I was happy to get a good update out for you all. The new cave biomes worked out pretty well, and seem to be working.

The issues with the chasm I left last week were very easily resolved, so I started working on the ability to be knocked down chasms. I think this is a fun feature, and more importantly, it's going down the path of more dynamic combat. One problem I have with a lot of traditional roguelikes is what I call the "noodle fight". Noodle fights happen when you attack an enemy and get locked in combat for several turns where the only rational move is to hit the enemy. While there is a time an place for hitting an enemy, a few features could be added to spice this up a bit. One of these for me was knockback. Knockback temporarily disengages the fight, and gives the player a bit of space to make a choice, which may involve running away, using a ranged or thrown weapon, waiting, or re-engaging. The new knockback behavior I added in '72a adds another element of randomness to this, so that you may have new opportunities or dangers when attacking repetitively. It also makes knockback more likely, so these choices will come up 150% more often.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/28b1efdfe050e0fd18a796a412119f0b5941a6fc.png[/img]
[i]Careful.[/i]

Since I was in the neighborhood, I changed around some sign behavior. Now, signs spawn not only in intersections, but in "exit" grids of towns and all the new biome features. These will help you orient yourself better and show you what is nearby. I also played around with the display code and made them fit what was written on them.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/d37ee0dc893b3475bbccfd781a0378bbf9076df2.png[/img]
[i]A much nicer sign.[/i]

And my goal over the next week is to restore a lot of lost functionality, particularly around towns, and provide some additional visual updates. I started on a new paradigm for generating stores and stuff in towns, which should be more stable. Now towns are guaranteed to have at least one food store, and depending on the number of houses they have, they can have a few more. These stores will also be guaranteed to be different kinds of stores.

In the time since I made the old store interface a long time ago, I developed a lot better ways to display interactions, so I started working on creating interesting-looking but functional interfaces for store. My goal for these are to make them appear more as I imagine them to be rather than an abstraction. It will take a lot more time to work on these panels, but I think they will be worth it. They'll allow me to better guide the player's imagination when exploring the world.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/42810fa6de7bdc5fe5aaf8260d2871013bda6996.png[/img]
[i]The new inn interface. The third bottle from the left is canonically Bombay Dry Gin.[/i]

Next week I should have updated interfaces for all the other shops, as well as a few other buildings added back into towns, and in the near future, I am going to add back in some quests. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com, or just leave them in the comments below.

notes.title: Devlog 72
notes.notes:
Writing this on Sunday, it didn't feel like I got a lot done, but looking back I accomplished some pretty significant stuff.

I decided to take the slightly diverted path of creating new environment generation. My three ideas were a fungal forest, an underground lake, and a chasm with a bridge. These would generate intermittently throughout the environment, following many of the same rules as towns and lairs follow.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/5fac6bd38a7615c8a020bce125df8aebe964d50f.png[/img]
[i]A view of a fully exposed map[/i]

notes.title: Update 0.2.71a / Devlog 71
notes.notes:
[h3]Changes[/h3]
[list]
[*]Added dice whist minigame to the game! Use the cheat command /whist to access it.
[/list]

Back from a retreat, and during the season of Lent I will ensure to redouble my efforts, and make sure I am spending a bit more time with the game.

This is a bit of a frivolous update, but every RPG needs a unique minigame that NPCs play. I quite like whist, and whist would be an appropriate game, but it can take a while to play. So to speed things up: dice whist. It is very close to whist, but since dice are independent, there is a lot more volatility. Is it a cliche to take a card game and transform it into a dice game for use in an RPG? Maybe, but I'm going to do it anyway.

The rules of dice whist are as follows: each player has six dice, all of which have different orientation of numbers (1-6) and suits (keys, coins, mushrooms). To start the game, a player draws one trump die out of a bag. This will decide what the players will play for, as well as which suit will be double-trump. They then draw trump dice out of a bag. The players who drew the double-trump dice roll, and the higher roll leads first overall. The lower roll leads last overall. The remaining players orient themselves in order of keys, coins, mushrooms, and keep the trump dice for play throughout the game.

The players then roll their dice, and keep them hidden. The starter initiates play, and players must follow suit if they have the option to. The highest, most recently played die wins the trick, unless a trump suit is played, where the highest most recently played die of the trump suit wins the trick. There are seven tricks per round, for each of the seven dice the players have (the six normal dice and the one trump die). Opposite side players are on the same team, and tricks are tallied accordingly.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/ff4d500946c0f1d59982b8c87b2e0d99fbbb4b8d.png[/img]
[i]My teammate led his trump die. Everyone must follow suit and play a coin if they have one.[/i]

There are four rounds per game, and each player will start one round. Trump suits rotate throughout the game, so that the starting player has a trump die of the trump suit for that round. At the end of the game, all the tricks are tallied up and the winner is declared. The team splits the pot, so each winning player doubles his ante.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/0d102389df90684f652e6a7f3ec61db3a30ba399.png[/img]
[i]An albino carrot well earned. Actually, my teammate had a lot of good rolls and carried the team.[/i]

While technically the minigame is not in the game, it can be accessed by typing "/" (the slash character) to enter cheat mode, and then typing the command "whist" (/whist). Again, maybe not the most significant thing to update, but I did have some fun making it and it probably will be in the final game, at least in some form. And the dice objects could be useful in other minigames, like dice poker.

I'd love to hear what you all think! Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com, or just leave them in the comments below.

[*]Added new ranged combat behavior: G (default) and right-click are for ranged weapons. T (default) and middle mouse button are for using thrown weapons

[*]Changed all "process" actions (such as eating, donning/doffing, quaffing) and new "process" actions like reloading into "interruptible process" actions. Moving or performing any other action will cancel the in-process action. Seeing an alerted enemy will not interrupt the process, but the player will have to manually continue the process by pressing the wait key (default period <.>) or by clicking on the player
[*]Reloading is a default process action behavior, and will happen automatically when a player is standing still and weapons need to be loaded.
[*]Swapping weapons between hands is now an interruptible process action with a cost of 5 seconds. This number was ascertained experimentally by myself using real weapons
[/list]


[h3]Bugfixes[/h3]
[list]
[*]Fixed towns spawning in cave dead ends
[*]Fixed saving to include the entire game world
[*]Fixed some glitches where key-based processes did not line up with mouse-based processes
[/list]

[h3]Known issues[/h3]
[list]
[*]Very occasionally stalagmites spawn outside of caves
[*]Probably few monsters will respawn in lairs
[/list]

Finally managed to get the update out this week, and after writing the changelog, it was actually a lot of stuff. So I'll have a bit of a running commentary about features I added this week.

The changeover to a cave-based system was going smoothly, but I noticed that some of the foods didn't really make sense anymore since your average plant just doesn't grow in a cave. Bioluminescent mushrooms do, however! So I changed around some of the green to a lightish blue, and voila! More sensible vegetable matter.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/870308f10afda3691631a00196dcbdcd1ddc779b.png[/img]
[i]It also looks cooler[/i]

The inventory system also got wrapped up these last few weeks. Players are now limited to 20 items, so make them count. Also, to prevent inventory bloat, you can now drop items.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/6679c23e331235b735c63fc2aa2102141329fa2b.png[/img]
[i]Everything should display correctly, but it's possible I missed an edge case somewhere[/i]

You'll notice that there is a new displayed inventory slot, called the belt. I'm still going back and forth on what role it ought to play, but for now it exclusively holds (an unlimited amount of one type of) thrown items. And that brings up another point: the "Target" control has been renamed "Throw", and I added a new control "Shoot" (default G). These refer to using thrown weapons and ranged weapons, respectively.

This is a good time to explain the revamped combat system. The old system focused on switching between right and left hand to attack with different items. The new system will focus on having the appropriate weapon in the appropriate hand at the start of combat. Attacks with the left hand will not receive bonuses. All ranged weapons now have limited effective ranges, and attempting to shoot things beyond the effective range means that you'll have a greater chance of missing (scaling with distance) and roll for damage with disadvantage. All ranged weapons now have magazines which have a limited amount of ammo and take a certain amount of time to be reloaded. You can manually reload items by clicking on them in the inventory, or otherwise they will reload automatically when you wait for sufficient time.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/96b8697e4997c689324e15158285af14dc0ab096.png[/img]
[i]Stuck reloading after missing a few times[/i]
These changes make the combat system more oriented towards planned-out combat, rather than a more typical wet noodle fight until the player or the enemy are dead. I'm planning a few more changes to make fights more dynamic and exciting, but those will come slightly later.

Finally, I added a time-based process system to replace the older time-cost action system. What does this mean in practice? Say you're getting a new weapon out of your inventory. Suddenly, a monster appears. Do you keep pulling it out, or do you fight with what you have on hand? The previous time-cost action system meant that you don't have a choice, and you would just get hit a bunch of times and perhaps die. The new process system allows you to choose. Most of the time, it won't make much of a difference, but in combat, it certainly will. Taking things out of your inventory, putting things back in your inventory, swapping your left and right hand, eating, drinking tonics, crafting items, and of course reloading are processes now. This was a feature some were asking for, and it's a good feature that gives players more freedom and makes combat more interesting, so it was worth adding.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/7b2a5897bc7170bd7b3e110903e8b4ea92214e31.png[/img]
[i]It's safest to eat big meals in towns, since they take a while to eat[/i]

We'll see what I get after this week. I'm most likely going to restart work with the towns to add NPCs back and get some quests going, but I might also add some additional cavern types in the cave system. I'd also like to hear some feedback on whether ammo should be stored in a special persistent item rather than directly in the inventory. notes.title: Devlog 67
notes.notes:
I managed to actually push the bugfix patch this week so I'm pretty happy with how the week turned out. Almost everything I wanted to achieve got done, so I will run through that before sharing what the next steps are.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/baebe7e4099fd86cf0039005b8c2ce88ffab72e6.png[/img]
[i]Towns are now named on the map! Highly convenient.[/i]

Some good quality of life things happened which look trivial, but were actually pretty difficult to implement, namely the signposts and the new mob vision code. Signposts now are useful and point toward places of interest nearby and report the distance as well. This took a lot of fixing and testing, but I'm pretty sure it all works very well now. Signs spawn at intersections, and since there may be several items of note in a direction, it chooses the closest. At worst, there may be as little as one thing on the sign.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/287df4b8e2199440fd6dd505429f962e86f6c2a4.png[/img]
[i]Distances are measured in furlongs because they actually were the most reasonable measurement. Fun fact: there are exactly 125 game tiles to the furlong.[/i]

I also did a lot of code maintenance and deleted a lot of stuff which no longer was useful due to the adoption of the tech test.

I packaged the totally essential things in this week's patch. The other stuff will come soon, probably after next week sometime. I want to make caves more interesting, so I'm going to cannibalize the old grid encounter system to create nice cave encounters. If you haven't seen a grid encounter, that's fine, because it was based on a prediction system to determine where the player could be if he kept traveling in the same direction. The great thing about a cave is that there is one likely direction the player will take, and where the player will be in the direction of travel is highly predictable.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/905390f2cc4ce2c7e4ccddac4d501ee35546d9f0.png[/img]
[i]Stalagmites in caves. They will provide cover against monsters one day, I'm sure.[/i]

There will also be monster respawns in lairs. This system will probably be linked to the previous system in some way that isn't yet obvious to me, but will come in due time. The purpose of this system is to make travel, particularly between floors, to be wildly more difficult than it currently is.

Finally, I'm looking at changes to the ranged weapons system. Right now, it is a bit overly complex with many different ammunition types. In addition, the no-reload system allows players with a lot of ammo to plink monsters from great distances. And maybe you should be able to, but it must come with certain costs.

In the future, ranged weapons will have four types of ammunition: pistol, rifle, shotgun, and galvanic cells.  Each ranged weapon will have an ammunition capacity and a reload speed. The player will by default not reload while in combat (since this could take several turns), and will by default reload after combat. Hit probability will fall off with distance and be relative to the weapon.

The purpose of these changes is to simplify while changing the ranged combat system into something like a first strike to soften enemies, rather than a sustainable tactic for picking off mobs. That will come in a couple of weeks though, so keep an eye out. This created a diffusion of caves as the layer increased, until it reached an approximate equilibrium. That wouldn't be so much of a problem but the equilibrium was not dense enough.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/17377449bca2f1976b52d8419bc3aa20eb2c1685.png[/img]
[i]This is what the industry would call "a major problem"[/i]

A secondary reason was that it makes the cave system more compact and consistent, because the cave system could be generated initially and the lairs added later on, as opposed to the previous way I was doing things.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/11b92079c3fda77b2d3da995ea0c2b69253d4683.gif[/img]

notes.title: Devlog 64
notes.notes:
I got a lot of stuff done this week, and made some good progress towards the tech test. To answer the question: can I get an MVP for the next version out before Christmas? I don't really know! It's about 50-50 right now, and dependent on time and stuff.

The first thing I knocked out was getting stores back in towns and getting them up and running. It was a pretty quick fix and a good thing to lead off with.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/900b55ae62d0aeb52c1570f450811946b89c65b6.png[/img]
[i]Same functionality as before. Sorry, no discounts.[/i]

I then elected to knock out some generation tasks. The planning phase which happened a few weeks ago was put into practice and everything worked really well, and the caves looked pretty natural.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/3f942c4627b6f4a0ad0e68d4012d543b0402aed8.png[/img]
[i]An example of a branching tunnel... and a choice to be made.[/i]

I had already intended to do some work with the minimap, which really needed an update, but my primary motive here was to get a clean, concise birds-eye view of the cave system. And my initial instincts for cave generation turned out to create a spaghetti-like morass of tunnels which was WAY too dense, allowing players to easily take alternative paths to areas.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/b877a191badda731f84e725044bd6a93819ebb64.png[/img]
[i]The extremely dense tunnel system.[/i]

The culprit: allowing tunnels to intersect to a small degree. Once I prohibited this, things looked quite a bit better.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/0a07dcad881f925e883af8d49bf4399945bd6cd6.png[/img]
[i]A less dense but still not perfect tunnel system.[/i]

The generation works by keeping track where the ends of the tunnels are, and generating there. However, since this would make a mostly-linear or branching cave, and I wanted a cyclic cave (a cave with closed loops), I also added a few more ways it can generate, leading to a much more balanced and realistic cave.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/9ecaf2331c001d0e0974e63a0d9a40f9768b085a.png[/img]
[i]Notice the arrow sections, which will one day create passageways to new depths of the cave.[/i]

Below is a diagram of the results which highlights a key feature I was intending to have in the generation. If the player wants to get between two particular towns, there are a few routes. The pink/red one takes him directly through a monster lair, which would be relatively dangerous, but might be necessary given certain constraints. In contrast the pink/blue path is far longer but far safer.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/0b0b443877686f82b78e551c7230523ac9779e5f.png[/img]
[i]While this effect isn't universal, it is more prevalent towards the edge of the map.[/i]

The tech test itself was a total success, and I'm 99% sure I'll move forward in this direction. The program uses roughly the same amount of memory as it did, and while the file sizes were seven times larger, they still are very manageable (115 KB) and not a concern.

Satisfied with generation for now, I turned to restoring some functionality to the lairs, since the paradigm shifted out from under them. Generation is back to working, and I'm working on restoring encounter and combat functionality.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/f33a5fb23740296165ce49e56c875998340446dc.png[/img]
[i]Already strongly resembling what once was.[/i]

I'll obviously return to a lot of things in the future, but I'll try to force out this update before Christmas, which give me two more days to work on this. We shall see...

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/77dff49a25628ebf6413f243977d0a26348cca74.png[/img]
[i]A fixed road.[/i]

Comparing this to the last previous screenshot might not seem like a very big or important difference, but it represents some big changes to how paths are generated within towns. In layman's terms, all the paths connect now, and moreover they're arranged in a way that's sensible given each town's particular generation within a cavern.

All in all, I'm pretty happy I spent the time I did arranging the towns. They are set up sensibly and don't look like they hold too strongly to a harsh grid pattern (even though they technically do). I spent the rest of the week engineering a few different farm plot layouts to get a little visual variety within towns.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/a02daf5c1ae97a6870e8b0b5239632177b67f225.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/c16fe7ea62261225de9b18f876f0daea082a162f.png[/img]
[i]A few views of the farms.[/i]

I might change a few things later on but this is good enough as a proof of concept to know they'll look okay the way they are.

I also managed to write out the algorithm for generating cave systems, and the initial results look promising, and I think I will manage to finish that part off in a few days, so I can spend the rest of the time on making the caves look nicer, both with wall and floor decorations/obstacles, as well as restoring some gameplay functionality to things like monster lairs and perhaps even NPCs to towns.

All in all, things are looking good for getting out an update before Christmas! The MVP for this update is: finished tech test, mapping, totally restored monster lairs, multilevel lairs leading into multilevel caves, and shops restored to towns.

notes.title: Devlog 62
notes.notes:
Got some good work done this week and the tech test is progressing smoothly.

The new town generation was causing several problems, mainly because there were so unanswered questions: should there be roads? how should towns be set up? how many houses should there be in towns?

The search to answer these questions was not terribly well documented with screenshots, but included some highlights such as generating towns exactly like monster lairs (but slightly more friendly), small sub-grids of houses, and little road grids.

Making the town resemble a monster lair just didn't make too much sense. The lairs were designed for each room to have one or more exit, for instance, and a small, sensibly designed house that a player can move through while still having some decoration should have only one exit. In addition, this didn't lend too well for having each house have some crop fields near it.

Sub-grids made the houses very regular, so I did a lot of playing around with the size and settled on 8x12. This allowed for a little play in the sideways direction and a lot of play in the back-and-forth direction. This led to some good variance. I had previously experimented with some road grids, and adding these back in proved to be a good idea, and brought some more coherence to the towns.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/e2694d5753a178904294939b9a854c6327d6398d.png[/img]
[i]Not quite there, but pretty close.[/i]

More variety will be returning to towns next week, since I'll have a bit more time to work on things. Following that, extensive generation and an actual tech test: determining if the file sizes are feasible with a very large area. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com, or just leave them in the comments below.

notes.title: Devlog 61
notes.notes:
Hey all, just came back from the field after a quick turnaround from a vacation with my girlfriend. It is also Advent once again, and the game is spiritually one year since Early Access release. It's a time for new beginnings, or at least reflection on the year that was and the year that will be. Speaking of which, what I have affectionately called "Tech Test 5" has been going extremely well.

Long story short: [i]Rogues of Europa[/i] is going underground, and I don't mean in some sort of figurative way. The overworld is being entirely replaced with an open-under-world. Rather than an infinite-ish plain, it will now take place in a giant cave system. This was not a frivolous decision. I think it will develop the lore of the game world in a more interesting way, and it will bring the player more immediately closer to where the action is, i.e., in the monster lairs, towers, and catacombs. I'll introduce these ideas by going through the development process a little bit.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/d73abcac03e1f8f788ea2016e352dbcf12c9a89a.png[/img]
[i]Totally removing the overworld. A bit scary, and not trivial.[/i]

The first thing I did was see how cave generation would work. I thought it would be possible using the grid system I had already been using for overworld generation. If you weren't already aware, this system is what causes farm fields to transition between different crops, fixes the locations of roads, and so on.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/53ff5fa7bdf699331af62da089cb4ca21ab679bf.png[/img]
[i]A map of the Mammoth Cave in Kentucky, overlaid with grid squares. This helped design what the cave would be like.[/i]

After looking at the cave map, I came up with a basic system for cave generation: as a path from gridsquare to gridsquare, moving back and forth more or less at random. This allowed me to minimize the storage size of a gridsquare to just a few bytes, which is good because I still want a very large map.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/a1d3aed6d13bb1e3fae46fc431ac7def9be8f014.png[/img]
[i]This cave segment is controlled by 4 numbers. The organic look is all procedural.[/i]

I then had a lot of tuning to do to make things render properly. I'm pretty sure it's all correct, but when I make a release be sure to keep a lookout for improperly generated terrain.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/f0c85b7df404d23d0f193db1413ada8a5005804f.png[/img]
[i]Each color represents a different rendering condition. Not every color is shown.[/i]

The results were very striking in my opinion. Generation, pathfinding, and rendering were all extremely fast, and the caves could be easily modified on the fly to create branching tunnels. From studying the cave diagram, this does happen quite frequently.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/1a7630b1e65befa490599bda93f7682a05af1ef1.png[/img]
[i]A branched tunnel.[/i]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/8dd00ae614ec89cb2f4164a698733b6e15774c20.png[/img]
[i]Donut tunnel! Donut tunnel! Donut, donut, donut, donut tunnel![/i]

After the success in the caves, I started to force all other generation into the grid paradigm (because it wasn't before). And it's been progressing with varying degrees of success, but I have full confidence everything will turn out.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/2dbb1941bd7ff259e992ddc42b5d1e4bf80b3d3b.png[/img]
[i]An early proof of concept demonstrating room generation within gridspace.[/i]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/ae95728313c3c89e4ddd033adc4fe40bce39508b.png[/img]
[i]A proof of concept demonstrating passage between caves and lairs.[/i]

I also had some good success generating caverns, which interestingly enough is the exact mathematical opposite of a tunnel.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/3ddce1facb52c49ca5bcc5b507268f6b04fa0ab2.png[/img]
[i]Underground towns, lakes, and fields will one day go in caverns.[/i]

I'll just need a little more figuring to make sure the new plan is viable. If it does something insane like make 8GB save files, I might have to do some reconsidering. If not, I think this will be the direction moving forward. For next week, I will work on creating towns (for the third time - ugh) and with a bit of luck the tech test will be complete, and I will make the final determination of the direction I want to go in.

I'd love to hear all of your feedback on Tech Test 5, especially criticism. Leave it in the comments here, or send an email to roguesofeuropa@protomail.com. I'll do my best to have a playable version out there soon which will have many of the main features that the previous version had. Ideally this will happen before Christmas.

notes.title: Devlog 60
notes.notes:
This week, I worked on timely events. The concept of a timely event is to have some sort of event (typically a monster appearance) happen at a certain time of day, requiring the player to wait around for it in order to witness and/or do something about it. Of course, this requires several subsystems in order to work properly.

Due to the fact that the game has a limited perspective, the player needs an alerting system so that off-screen events can be identified. This was a long time coming, as I had originally intended for them to take place in monster lairs, so that the player could identify when a patrolling mob was coming along, or when a player-placed tinkering device got triggered. So I developed a decent-looking sound wave effect which took forever to get to look right. I had to cheat the "font" grid a little bit to do so, which is unfortunate, but I'm in charge here, so I make the rules.

I have also been countenancing an internal debate I had a while ago, very early into the development of [i]Rogues of Europa[/i]. I won't bother getting into the details right now, because there are many, but it would represent a particularly dramatic change to the overall flow of the game. It would still be recognizable, but there would be enormous changes, particularly in how everything generates. I really don't know if it is workable, more efficient, or produces a better experience, but I have a good gut feeling about it, and I think it's worth testing. It's something I'm at least going to test out in the next few weeks by forking my existing project. I at least don't anticipate things taking too long to test out, and I will make my final determination then. But I'll keep you all posted with results and thoughts as I proceed. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com, or just leave them in the comments below.

notes.title: Devlog 59
notes.notes:
Bit of a slower week this week as I created more and more systems to improve the quests. We're getting to the point where enough will be done to more rapidly create quests when all the modular systems are in place.

The first new system I added was a learning system. This allows the player to learn certain information about the quest (which I guess you could already do in your head) and display it in the quest screen. Highly convenient! It also requires you to ask around town for information. In the future, it will take both clue-finding, interviewing, and reasoning to determine accurate information about the quest, but for now, you get a nice report about the pertinent information in the quest screen.

Since monsters can now be clues that lead back to a nest or other group of monsters, I added little pips to the minimap where you combated monsters, as well as a history on the side to tell you which monsters were encountered where.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/7ab6ac32ab66e8d4af3a06c401c295e85a2937d3.png[/img]
[i]Marked improvements in the quest display.[/i]

I also developed this nice prison building that I will use in some variants of the monster encounter quest.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/fc2808236159bd7bdd3d315aac2ae6bc13cda795.png[/img]
[i]The key was dropped by a boss monster, naturally.[/i]

It's the little things that often turn out to be massive hassles. For example, you might recognize the key and locked door system from the underground cultist temple catacombs. However, they had to be basically entirely remade in order to work in the overworld since all of the inner-workings relied on assumptions like the fact that they would be underground, there would be only a certain amount of doors that would need to be checked. That's not to mention the key itself, which actually is the first item dropped as the result of a monster kill. In hindsight, probably more items should do that.

On the docket for next week: more complex quest information and interactions, time-based events (i.e., monsters attacking at certain times). I also will do some experimenting with new NPC behavior, which will include some of the first inklings of the companion system. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com, or just leave them in the comments below.

notes.title: Devlog 58
notes.notes:
I have been diligently working on the new quest system this week. Yet it seems like every time I want to add a new feature, something else crops up which feels more urgent.

I started on a few conversations, but then I realized I needed a few additions to the token system for variability. There were a few setbacks here, and I went on to make a few conversations with the new features. Now, all conversation elements can use the token system, and I added something called "spintax". Spintax was invented for email marketing to add some variety to emails so they could say the same thing without saying the [i]exact[/i] same thing. In the context of conversations, it will make it so the player won't be able to effectively remember conversations between playthroughs, unless he's really paying attention.

Armed with the new conversations, I started on some of the quest generation, but I realized it would need to wait because I wanted the quest screen to be revamped a little bit. Previously, it was quite lacking in features, full of bad information, glitchy, and also gave away far too much. The redesign is well under way however.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/5392b300463a43541c441e84663793c1de58ba36.png[/img]
[i]Nothing final here, but still some interesting things to talk about.[/i]

There is now a generated quest description text which doesn't spoil anything about the quest you haven't discovered yet. I also modified the minimap to be more reliable and to give out some great information, such as where you've found clues and accurate road locations, as well as making some general rendering improvements to it.

I should have plenty of time next week, and I hope to push through and release the redesigned quest. Again, this will just be one quest in one town, but it will be a stepping stone to more impressive things, and as a proof of concept, it will pave the way for bigger updates faster. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com, or just leave them in the comments below.

notes.title: Devlog 57
notes.notes:
After wrapping up some bugfixes early in the week, I went on to start on the new quest system.

Naturally, this hit a massive wall when I determined that it was going to go nowhere until conversations were revamped a little bit. So I added a few conversations, and reengineered them to accept a variety of new inputs. If you weren't already aware, the conversation system is designed to have mad-libs style entries so that a relatively low amount of conversation types (probably around 30 or so) will be able to handle all quests.

I might need to do some playing around with my working schedule in order to write more, but I think I can squeeze in a little writing at work, which will allow me to finish them faster than I have been.

I additionally added a system to reinforce the "monster of the week" gameplay concept, in which all of the people in a town become people you can ask about the quest. Most of them don't know anything, of course, but they can help lead you towards some witnesses who actually do know some things. After you find and question witnesses, these clues will be entered into the quest screen (which some have pointed out is relatively lacking), and can be referenced from then on, and used to figure out not only where the objectives are, but some good information on when and how to go about achieving the objectives.

Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com.

notes.title: Devlog 55
notes.notes:
Despite some setbacks and having to work later this week, I did manage to almost get that tinkering system ready. All the panels are now done, and I started on the tinkering screen and implementation.

I was able to make several innovations this week which will have more exciting implications. First off, I made the mode-switching code more consistent, which should lead to less bugs or glitches due to switching between modes (e.g., from the game to the quest screen and back). While I haven't 100% capitalized on this (and maybe never will) it will lead to more efficient and effective code in the future. In addition, I can now apply filters to the inventory, which will likely have positive implications for the future. This dovetails with the smart-use item system where the inventory itself will also do what the player wants, such as filtering for weapons when the player is selecting something for his hand slots or filtering for armor when the player is selecting something for his armor slot.

And I applied these two systems to the tinkering system, which you can see below.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/43d118843fa86a5cea632f3be8cd1eb0cb193847.png[/img]
[i]Tinkering what is essentially a claymore landmine.[/i]
The system allows for up to three items to be crafted together. In this case, I'm adding explosives, fragments, and a radio trigger, which will allow me to place the tinkered item down and detonate it later when I activate the trigger. Pretty convenient when drawing monsters through a choke point.

Also, since it's a pet peeve of mine, the tinkering slots remain filled with items even if the player navigates away from the screen, since the tinkering system represents thinking, in a sense. If you had an idea for something, you may not think about it temporarily and put it away for a bit, but as soon as you think about crafting again, it should pop right to the top of your head.

Hopefully I can get that update out later this week, but I might be held longer at work this week. It's a bit of a busy time as the end of the fiscal year approaches. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com.

notes.title: Devlog 54
notes.notes:
I was working on a bit more life stuff this week, so not too much got done in [i]Rogues of Europa[/i]. However, I do have a desk now, which should improve my productivity. I'm almost all moved in now.

The goal with the tinkering system is to not have a "meta" tinker weapon to deploy, but rather encourage situational weapon deployment based on what parts the player has access to.

I have also added an autosave feature this week. The game will autosave when the "curtains" fall (i.e., when the player goes up or down stairs, goes on a train, sleeps, and so on). I will add a feature to have a time-based autosave which will save every so often (user-defined), because you may want autosaves when just walking around. The saving will take a short but noticeable amount of time, so it will very slightly disrupt play, but you will have the option to turn it off or reduce it's frequency if it becomes annoying to you.

notes.notes:
Just a quick devlog this week. I'm in the process of moving to a new apartment so things are a bit hectic, but I've made some good progress.

First off, thanks to det for finding a few bugs. I haven't pushed out a patch for them since the gameplay will change relatively drastically in the next update I'm planning, but they technically will be fixed in the next update, for what it's worth. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com.

notes.title: Devlog #51
notes.notes:
The first steps in the new direction start this week.

Welcome to Wightbarrow. This will be the testing environment going forward, and the only town on the map. Again, this isn't really traditionally roguelike, but I'm just dialing things back for the purposes of testing so that something good might eventually grow out of it.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/09502f029b2465df1f9d4880a8f752a25cd176d9.png[/img]
[i]Yes, I know.[/i]

I spent the week writing out the new quest system on paper so it can be implemented. While there will be the same basic quest types, they will now have relatively different courses they can take, making them more unique. I made a system for the monster nest quests that alters four variables in a decision tree, resulting in over 30 unique looking quests, thanks to the power of, well, exponents ironically enough. 

I also remembered as I was developing the quests that I wanted a tinkering system, so I will probably implement that next week. The basic idea is allowing players to create "inventions" which take special crafting ingredients and debuff or damage enemies depending on what kind of ingredients are used. Look out for more development in this area in the next week.

The testing environment will ensure that things stay relatively consistent and easy; there's no sense in walking several miles to test a quest. I will make periodic releases of the testing environment, to make sure that you all are happy with the quests and how they are conducted.

I will determine how practical it is to get them all implemented, then make an estimate of how long things will take to release an update. While the tinkering system will probably be finished next week, I really have no idea how long it will take to develop the new quest system and implement it. But I will continue to release (mostly) weekly updates. And as always, put any prayer requests, questions, or comments you have in the comments section, or shoot me an email at roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com. I promise to check frequently!

notes.title: Devlog #50 and Update 0.2.50a
notes.notes:
The art update isn't heading to a dramatic finish, but I think it will be a promising one. I finished up a few music things and added them. I decided on the music burst option, which I added in a few key places, though I might add a percussion or muted running track underneath in the future.

Following some mentorship I received, I will focus moving forward on improving the story elements, trying to create a small slice of the game as effective as possible. This will consist of going deeper with conversations, clues, and interactions in towns.

The first things I will look at will be town generation. I've made it clear that part of the inspiration for [i]Rogues of Europa[/i] comes from "monster of the week" television shows, and I want to return to that to emulate. This will mean smaller, closer towns, designed to look more unique and having singular problems, rather than the virtually identical towns with four quest givers. The initial phases will be more limited tests, and they won't even be rogue-like. As the version develops, it will bloom back into procedural generation, and the towns will return to difference and randomness.

I know this isn't really sticking to the plan I had, but I'm still new to this and I think this will be a better direction to take. But it should be close enough to keep things reasonably on track and in the right direction, and the gameplay will be back to advancing.

I'd love to hear any feedback you, the players, have as to the new direction. Leave it in the comments, or email it to me at roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com, along with any other questions or prayer requests you may have.

From my experimentation it's really easy to get off the rails into the deep end of difficulty (such as a puzzle that takes well over 15 minutes to solve) or way into the shallow end (such as a puzzle that gets solved by chance).

My goal as I've mentioned is to have puzzles that can be solved reasonably fast through logic or algorithms, or somewhat fast through brute force methods. The light puzzle in its current state can't be done through the former. notes.title: DEVLOG #35
notes.notes:
I started off this week by working on the logic gate puzzle. The main problem I was dealing with was the fact that there were a lot of ways to solve the puzzle, usually approaching around 10% of possible solutions. This number was around 25-50% typically before I added some code which recast everything if that number was too big.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/eb29ba85a624f322fae156b7585c97f0e43f3b39.png[/img]
[i]I got 9 problems, but a switch ain't one.[/i]

You can imagine the puzzle as a combination lock with 9 binary digits. The problem here lies in the fact that only 3 of the digits are relevant, and they are only partially related to the other digits. The goal is to make every single digit relevant.

So, as I typically do, I radically redesigned the puzzle. Rather than controlling gates, the player controls switches. I decided on only six switches, or 64 combinations. The logic gates are static and hidden from the player, and now draw from a pool of every possible binary logic gate. Unlike before, there is only one possible solution (approximately 20% of generated puzzles result in one solution, which is an acceptable rate for regeneration).
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/d19fa3c7a63e95024ecd22fab6a3672008de14f0.png[/img]
[i]This took about a minute for me to solve, which is an good amount of time for the complexity.[/i]

Now the puzzle is at least fair and challenging, and it requires a good amount of experimentation. It doesn't require knowing what a logic gate is or how they work, but can be figured out just with a bit of trial and error. That said, knowing how logic gates work and having a bit of pen and paper could allow you to solve the puzzle more quickly.

For you speedrunners or perfectionists out there (but I repeat myself), the puzzle is scrambled so that either two, three, or four switches need to be flipped to solve the puzzle. Later on when I finalize this puzzle, I will incorporate some sort of "bleed valve" which can summon a monster if the player is flipping too many switches. This will encourage thinking rather than brute force.

I then began working on my planned "hotwiring" puzzle. Much like the name suggests, this puzzle will look like a breaker box or a phone switchboard, with wires going everywhere. The goal is to make the proper connections to open the door. Making the wrong connections will do things like set off alarms, release monsters, or shock the player.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/5b68ad651908c3de01bd4ddb69d7b18ff13da9db.png[/img]
[i]An early render, showing the wire colors and textures.[/i]

I was pretty happy with how the early render turned out. I made the wires distinct looking, with the color enhancing the experience, rather than defining it.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/afaa503a6aad72e5c3b9d29789090e5b2f1d1e5f.png[/img]
[i]Now that's more like it.[/i]

As I played through this puzzle, I realized it could be treated as a sorting puzzle, which tickled the small part of me that had fun in Data Structures I class. It's a solid puzzle though, and I like how it turned out.

I do plan on making more puzzles, perhaps more mathematical in nature, but I have at least enough to make a proof of concept within the towers. Besides, the 0.0.30a release is getting a bit stale and you good people deserve an update.

To round out the week and prepare for release, I then set to the task of integrating the puzzles with objectives and including other stuff in the mad scientist towers, such as monsters and loot.

notes.title: Lent
notes.notes:
The season of Lent begins today; a season of fasting, prayer, and almsgiving. Today's reading from the book of Joel exhorts us to "Rend your hearts, not your garments" (2:13). But what does that mean?

When we fast, it is the spiritual effects that are most important. For example, the purpose of fasting from food is not just to deprive yourself, but remind yourself that there are things more important than your physical needs. In more modern times, it has become popular to fast from things like social media, television, and so on. Again, this shouldn't be just about depriving yourself, but about reorienting your life to focus on God.

And when our hearts are rent open by fasting, there is room for prayer and works of charity to come in. Fasting should result in lasting changes to your spiritual life. Consider carefully this Lent what you would like to fast from, and what you would like the effects of that fasting to be.

notes.title: DEVLOG #34
notes.notes:
I started this week off with a bang by fixing the chemical puzzle (har har). After a bit of playtesting, I determined that the logic behind the game was far too opaque, making it too difficult to make an informed, logical conclusion from the information. So I changed up the game logic once again.

Now the logic is as follows: there are three different chemicals, informally "weak", "medium", and "strong". The goal of the puzzle is to find the two "medium" chemicals by mixing pairs together. Overall weak mixtures will make noise and sometimes summon a monster. Overall strong mixtures will blow up prematurely. Weak + strong mixtures will fizzle out, and only the medium + medium mixture will blow a hole in the door. The player can then make logical conclusions about the chemicals in the mixture from the narration text.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/81a7ea2186009d3ba96bf4f14a1107d8d7156ed4.png[/img]
[i]If you're in a lab long enough, you're gonna have an accident.[/i]

I then started work on another floor based puzzle, the promised logic gate puzzle. The premise of the puzzle is that the player will see several ports in the wall next to the door. The ports are either "high" or "low" voltage, indicated by a wide bright line or a narrow line. Several power sources are arrayed throughout the room as well as some logic gates. The goal is to match the ports to the inputs using the logic gates.

Each logic gate can be swapped between one of its two states. No information is given on which kind of logic gate they are, but they will be one of the three primary non-negated binary types (OR, AND, and XOR).
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/a996bcba2a81d38aa51d2b0c0e8f123332a4019d.png[/img]
[i]Wires and pylons.[/i]

Unfortunately, I didn't have enough time this week to finish everything with this puzzle. I'm not 100% happy with it since there are too many solutions to the puzzle, but I am confident I can work something out.

notes.title: DEVLOG #33

This week I started off with a bit of a rework on the puzzle I was doing last week.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/6d48222cbe76dd2d41173bbcc18781f8f7b9d0e8.png[/img]
[i]Imagine a barrier blocking you from the other side.[/i]

I implemented most of the things I was talking about, like the interactable buttons rather than the pressure plates, making the puzzle easier, and so on, but I still was not completely happy with it. The puzzle was often too easy. Perhaps that's partially because the meat of the puzzle is too easy, but that will become evident as I test it further. I shelved it for a bit because I was more inspired to work on a different puzzle this week.

The puzzle I came up with is technically just a code breaking puzzle, but with a more interesting skin on it. The player is presented with six chemical vessels and must find the correct combination of two of them to create an explosive to knock down a door in the center of the room. Each chemical has certain properties, and mixing them produces a new chemical with different properties. The player performs experiments and gains information to logically deduce which chemicals to mix.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/349fd5c3294cc226405738ebcd45081d70e2ca58.png[/img]
[i]An early proof of concept of the minigame screen.[/i]

While I initially had a more complicated version of this minigame where the player had to test for three different explosive effects, I created a much simpler version that has only one parameter. Each beaker is assigned a number. The goal is to reach a certain sum, and there's only one way to do it.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/620f9466befadd2a2e5d57c7e0ea30eeb6acb9fb.png[/img]
[i]True to form, the beakers, colors, and order will be randomized.[/i]

The math experts among us will note that there are only 15 possible combinations of two chemicals, so you could in theory brute-force this in a short amount of time if you're systemic. Excellent point. This is why I added some penalties. If the sum is too low, then there's a chance the shattering glass summons a monster. If the sum is too high, then the mixture blows up in your hand. It pays to pay attention.
