notes.title: DEVLOG #31
notes.notes:
Sorry for the missed week last week. I was very ill and not in any state to work or even type out a devlog. However I have recovered fully and will resume pushing out weekly devlog once again.

This couple of weeks was spent working on the mad scientist towers, particularly implementing the physical spaces the puzzles would occupy.

My initial instincts for making towers was just a big square. Plenty of room for activities, so to speak, reasonably sized, nice and utilitarian.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/c731761e523cd581a81dc9fb238e22418f9931ee.png[/img]
[i]Like father, like son.[/i]

I might put some mobs inside the rooms, or loot drops or something. But the real meat and potatoes are obviously going to be the puzzles.

Much like in monster lairs, mad scientist towers will have a randomly generated set of encounters on each floor. This will probably either be two puzzles which must be solved to advance (one door puzzle and one floor puzzle) or some monsters and a door puzzle.

As I made my building, which has a relatively complex interior, I finally got absolutely fed up with the previous way I had been doing pathfinding in the overworld. I fixed up an extremely inefficient cost function and implemented A* instead of the previous greedy algorithm. Now everything uses A*. If you're an indie developer out there, write this down: do things the right way, not the easy way. If you just play the game, you will likely see some slight pathing changes which are guaranteed to be the most efficient route, making your moves take slightly less time. The previous greedy algorithm could enter infinite loops, which happened more frequently in challenging geometry, but the new A* algorithm is guaranteed to terminate.

I then started making the actual levels of the tower. I'm planning on having a more open plan than the ground floor (the ground floor itself may change). From the player perspective, the tower is fundamentally the same as a lair. It only goes up or down in your imagination. With that in mind, I just copied existing code, and after a few tweaks, got tower levels to generate.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/b51791647eb488e3c2f762e1116e2a7d53ccd795.png[/img]
[i]Turns out mob generation was still turned on. From the program's perspective, the tower is merely a special case of lair with only one room and no paths.[/i]

I fixed the mob generation issue and got on to creating an actual level for the tower. My plans for the towers are to have a primary room or set of rooms (decided as an encounter) and a secondary room which leads to the stairs up. This room will be blocked off with a locked door.

The clock will be ticking as you solve puzzles which means that monsters will encroach on you as you solve them. It might be a good idea to fight them off first. Any damage taken while in a puzzle will automatically end the puzzle.

My goal is to have the towers wrapped up and a good update out by the end of January, so keep on the lookout for that. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com.

notes.title: DEVLOG #30
notes.notes:
(Before I start off here, I'd like to know what you as the players want to see in these devlogs. I've been doing more long-form, narrative commentary, but if you want something different, please tell me in the comments.)

After pushing update 0.0.30a, I immediately started working on 0.1: Towers and Temples. Therefore I had a decision: towers or temples? I decided to choose towers because I felt more inspired to do them.

My concept for a mad scientist tower from the start was to have a puzzle based dungeon. But which puzzles? My goal with puzzle design here is to have it be maybe one or two steps above a Wordle puzzle. Somewhat difficult, easy to get wrong if you don't know what you're doing, but definitely a less-than-five-minutes type of puzzle. Something like a full sudoku puzzle or even a crossword would be much too long. Another consideration is accessibility. When I say accessibility I'm not talking about arachnophobia mode or games-journo easy mode, but rather colorblind accessibility. 8% of the male population (so roughly 7% of gamers) are colorblind to some degree, making catering to the colorblind roughly the same as catering to the left-handed. This means puzzles where colors may be featured, but aren't essential.

Ideally, I want a mix of "door puzzles," which are encounter-driven puzzles produced by interacting with doors (much like hacking in many games), and "spatial puzzles," movement or interaction-based puzzles based on object interaction or NPC movement (much like Zelda-style puzzles). Likely these puzzles will punish you for taking too long or entering an incorrect answer.

The first puzzle I made I called the "steam lock." Basically it's a lockpicking puzzle. The pins must be activated in a certain order in order to work, and this must be determined experimentally. For example, if the true order is {5, 3, 4, 1, 2}, and the player chooses to activate pin 1 first, the only pin that can be activated after that is pin 2. However, if the player chooses to activate pin 3 first, he can activate pins 1, 2, or 4 after that. 
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/21b526404b08ad5082a847a5d76643f10fb738fd.png[/img]
[i]An early, slightly too easy version of the steam lock.[/i]

After determining it was a bit too easy, I split the pistons in half and added a middle state to the valves. This was not as serious as doubling the amount of pins to solve for, since it's a guarantee that pin 1b comes after pin 1a. I decided to time myself to determine whether it was too hard or not. With the use of pen and paper, I was able to solve one such puzzle in 101 seconds. Without the benefit of pen and paper, I solved another puzzle in 147 seconds. Both times benefited from a mental algorithm I invented to solve the problem quicker, which I will leave to the community to figure out. Either way, this is probably a good amount of difficulty to puzzle through. The worst case here is I have to vary or reduce the number of pin sets, but that's a problem for another time.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/393c3ff90422d572a6ea362892ae56db80b53144.png[/img]
[i]The new, improved, and much more difficult steam lock.[/i]

The next puzzle I decided to make is what I've always called a "light-switch puzzle" in my mind. I'm sure it has a formal name, but whatever. The basic idea is there is a series of lights which are controlled by switches. Each switch inverts the state of some lights and not others. The goal is to turn on all the lights. This would have to wait though, because I wanted to make this one the Zelda-style interaction type puzzle, meaning I would need an actual dungeon to be in. So the rest of the week was spent on getting an entirely new dungeon generating, as well as working on my car, which needed some maintenance this week.

I did manage to discover and squish a bug. This was quite an important one because it was a mathematical function that several pathfinding functions relied on. Oops.

Next week, I will finish up the actual towers and push out a release. I have reconsidered not releasing the update till it's ready, since I want some other people to test out the puzzles and make sure they're not too hard or too easy. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com.

notes.notes:
Finally, I've made some good progress towards the "Towers and Temples" update. After putting out the majority of the fires from the initial release, things are getting good to go, and getting back in the swing of adding content.

I decided this week to implement an unusual mechanic. This new mechanic allows time to progress just by standing around, turning the game into a real-time game. However, the time stops progressing when the player is in danger. In addition, the time progresses faster when the player is moving, that is, the normal speed it was progressing while moving (approximately 30 in-game seconds per second).

Why have I decided to do this? It just felt more natural to me. Now, instead of the whole world just going on pause when you stop moving, things can just naturally happen around you. I plan on it leading to other things such as getting interrupted while looking at your inventory in a dungeon, or making a decision in an encounter.

Speaking of which, this week I added encounters to the overworld. Not only will this make monsters roam the overworld, but it will also add the NPC-style encounters from lairs to random spots in the overworld. It's been a bit of a lighter week for me because I've had a lot of stuff going on, particularly additional choir practices and working on an update to another game. However, I was still able to push out some stuff.

Customizable controls were added this week. Please, tell me if the interface is not working for you. In related news, I added a new control set for users who prefer to use a number pad, bringing the total number of control sets up to three. You can customize each one how you like, but the amount of options for defaults should make that task a lot easier on you.

The bugs on the docket this week were a few nagging bugs in lairs. Particularly, faster monsters didn't look like they were getting pushed back because of the logic surrounding how player turns worked. Now, any mob must wait for its turn until all narration blocks are gone.

Formerly, the flow went:
[list]
[*]Land a blow on the monster and push it back
[*]A narration pops up that the monster has been pushed back
[*]The monster moves toward the player
[*]The player closes out the narration
[/list]
Now the flow goes:
[list]
[*]Land a blow on the monster and push it back
[*]A narration pops up that the monster has been pushed back
[*]The player closes out the narration
[*]The monster moves toward the player
[/list]
This simple change actually had a great side effect of allowing the player to control when the monsters take their turn in basically all situation, which improves the perception of game flow, in my opinion.

I also fixed a few rendering bugs involving running away from monsters in tunnels. Previously, you wouldn't be able to see monsters in certain situations. Scary!

And finally, I've received some feedback that the traditional English coinage system is a bit opaque to understand. My first thought was, "That's a good thing." But I relented and made color-coding in shops, inns, and railway stations to more descriptively show you how many of what type of denomination you're spending. notes.title: DEVLOG #22
notes.notes:
I started off this week by actually implementing XP, something that was a long time coming. Whenever you level up, you will gain an amount of hit points equal to 1d6+5 which is hopefully well balanced since those numbers came out of the top of my head with no basis. The amount of XP to level up is an exponential equation with slow growth: 10 * level ^ 1.4. Since level is currently capped out at 20, the first level is 10 XP, and the final level is 616 XP, and a total of 5187 XP must be gained to fully level up.

I've mentioned effects in passing once or twice, probably, but this week I actually implemented them. Now, you can do exciting things like:

[list]
[*] Get wasted on tonics
[*] Get frightened by monsters
[*] Eat yourself sick
[*] Exhaust yourself from staying up all night in a monster lair
[/list]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/76f6766201e7f23f1caa9971c8667112159c4a13.png[/img]
[i]You also aren't allowed to eat the same thing all the time.[/i]

These effects happen naturally over the course of the game or from decisions you make. And they will have major in-game consequences if you can't rectify them. For example, if you're too scared, you shake a bit and can't aim straight, or if you're too tired, you can't fix your weapons as effectively.

Speaking of which, weapons now get dented, dinged, and scratched when they're used. I've yet to balance weapon repairing, but generally it's easier to repair a simpler weapon.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/ace3a850d22a141f1fe8c4def1f05bfdf356dbec.png[/img]
[i]It's a good idea to stock up on weapons in case this happens.[/i]

I added healing this week. Previously, the player got no healing and liked it. Seriously though, I was always planning on adding it but never took the time to do so because I was busy iteratively playtesting and didn't need healing. Healing is probably most similar to Minecraft. It happens reasonably quickly, and costs additional hunger. It's impossible to heal if you're experiencing any level of hunger. In addition, healing has other costs, like increasing your exhaustion, distracting you, and so on.

I also played around this week with other game features and bugfixing, such as monsters waking each other up, making sure dungeons can be entered and exited, and having the player spawn in with some food.

And finally, I should finish the trailer by close of business tomorrow. You can guess when exactly that will be, how exciting! Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com.

notes.title: DEVLOG #21
notes.notes:
Given the Holy Days this week, I was quite busy. But nonetheless I got some stuff done, and the beta release fast approaches.

Now, a variety of shops spawn in towns, not just food shops. I'm not 100% sold on how they spawn, and more importantly which items are in their menus, but they still are out there and you can buy stuff.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/d01262d4ec1ecb438b02a750997679e3b2bc2058.png[/img]
[i]The Tuxborough gun store. A fine establishment, which offers a derringer, a revolver, a sawn-off shotgun, and a .450 cal rifle.[/i]

I also added bosses to the game, though they are under-implemented at the moment. These more powerful monsters will be found at the end of lairs, and represent the objective of a lair quest.

This week I also added sacramentals, perhaps being inspired by the holy days. Sacramentals work exactly as they do in real life. They're tied to certain devotions, they improve your fortitude (that is, your willingness to continue), and on some occasions they are a physical reminder to yourself or others about your faith.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/d01262d4ec1ecb438b02a750997679e3b2bc2058.png[/img]
[i]I plan on having a lot of sacramentals to choose from.[/i]

Why did I make these specific design choices? I didn't want them to be some sort of cheap talisman or superstitious trick that grants some sort of buff or ward, because that's not how sacramentals work. They work as physical reminders of the metaphysical. Do you receive supernatural protection because you wear a red scapular in honor of Christ's Passion? No, unless God granted you that grace, and it would be superstitious and impious to think otherwise. Would another person treat you differently if he sees you holding a rosary? Yes, and a monster or demon even more so. Sacramentals will work similarly in the game, as subtle reminders and outward signs of faith, and while they won't be essential, they will be nice to have.

After that, I did a little bugfixing. Now, lairs and nests no longer spawn in rivers or on roads (assuming I did it right). While I'm planning on making rivers impassible or difficult to cross one day, now it just doesn't look ugly. I also made it so immovable, indestructible encounter-linked NPCs no longer spawn on top of level stairs, which means now there's a 100% guarantee that lairs are fully passable.

I then started on the "Challenge Rating" system for quests. This allows me to scale the difficulty of all quests throughout the game. How it works is that all monsters have a relative proportion they appear at each challenge rating, and a value by which that increases each level. This will allow me to do things like tweak when monsters first appear and how frequently they appear on later levels by changing a couple numbers. It also allows me to have non-integer challenge ratings, which allows for even more fine tuning.

For next week, I will still be working diligently on getting this initial beta release up, and you should expect a trailer soon as well, so keep an eye out for that. Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com.

notes.title: All Saints Day
notes.notes:
May the blessings of Jesus be upon you on this solemn feast day.
Regardless of where you are in life, always, always strive for holiness. The Communion of Saints is full of men and women who were the most awful sinners before they repented and changed their lives. It's never too late, and the best time to be holy is now.

I'd also like to extend a gentle reminder that today is a Holy Day of Obligation in the United States.
If you want to learn more about saints and All Saints Day, I recommend this resource: https://www.ewtn.com/catholicism/seasons-and-feast-days/all-saints-20377

notes.title: DEVLOG #20
notes.notes:
Finally, after a few roadblocks, Rogues of Europa now has a Steam Store page! Just in time for DEVLOG 20! This will be the first DEVLOG posted to both Steam and the website, which will be how it will be going forward.

I started out the week making some more encounters. They're quite fun to make. I want to have somewhere around 40 or 50 of them by the time I have a full release.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44727316/d5c50bc94672e0afeed42ae6b32de9832d11239c.png[/img]
[i]You'll notice a few formatting changes, as well as pretty colors in the panel. I realized the white ASCII art might be a bit boring.[/i]
I'm not gonna spoil the rest of the encounters I made, though.

I also produced another song this week, just a quick one, but one of my personal favorites. You can check that out on the website, [url=http://roguesofeuropa.com/2023/10/29/devlog-20/]here[/url].

Other than that, I was working on the Steam store page. It's been a bit of a lighter week, but still worthwhile. The first beta release will be coming soon! Remember to email any questions, comments, and prayer requests you have to roguesofeuropa@protonmail.com.
